chat_messages.text:
This is a rich theological thread that runs through both Testaments. Here's what's there, organized by the two halves of your question.

**God using imperfect tools**

Isaiah 10:5-15 — Assyria called "the rod of my anger," used to discipline Israel even though Assyria itself is arrogant and will later be judged. The clearest statement that God wields nations who don't know they're being wielded.

Isaiah 45:1-4 — Cyrus, a pagan Persian king, called God's "anointed" (messiah) and "my shepherd," explicitly told "though you have not known me." Used to free Israel from exile.

Habakkuk 1:5-11 — God raises up the Babylonians, called "that bitter and hasty nation," as his instrument despite their violence.

Numbers 22-24 — Balaam, a diviner-for-hire, made to bless Israel against his employer's wishes. And the donkey, used as a prophet when Balaam wouldn't see.

John 11:49-52 — Caiaphas, the high priest who orchestrated Jesus's death, prophesies truly without knowing it: "he prophesied not of himself."

2 Corinthians 4:7 — "We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us." The instrument is meant to be visibly inadequate.

1 Corinthians 1:27-29 — "God hath chosen the foolish things... the weak things... base things... things which are not, to bring to nought things that are."

**God making the unworthy worthy so they can serve**

Isaiah 6:5-8 — Isaiah cries "I am a man of unclean lips," coal touched to his mouth, iniquity purged, *then* "Here am I; send me." The cleansing precedes and enables the commission.

Jeremiah 1:6-9 — "I cannot speak: for I am a child." God touches his mouth: "I have put my words in thy mouth."

Exodus 4:10-12 — Moses pleads he is "slow of speech." God: "Who hath made man's mouth?... I will be with thy mouth."

1 Timothy 1:12-16 — Paul: "who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy... that in me first Jesus Christ might shew forth all longsuffering, for a pattern."

Ezekiel 36:25-27 — "I will sprinkle clean water upon you... a new heart also will I give you... and cause you to walk in my statutes." Worthiness installed, not earned.

1 Peter 2:9-10 — "Ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood... which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God."

Zechariah 3:1-7 — Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments, accused by Satan. "Take away the filthy garments from him... I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment." Then he's commissioned.

Romans 4 and the whole arc of Abraham — counted righteous before circumcision, before the law, before any qualifying act.

The pattern is consistent: the call doesn't wait for fitness, and the fitness, when it comes, is given rather than achieved. Want me to pull any of these into longer context, or trace a specific thread (prophets, kings, Gentile instruments)?

See the blessed attendants by whom his government is served. Above the throne stood the holy angels, called seraphim, which means "burners;" they burn in love to God, and zeal for his glory against sin.

content.title: Preach The Word In Season & Out Of Season (2 Timothy 4:2) - Bob Russell Ministries
content.text:
But I’m commissioned in Scripture to preach God’s Word, “in season and out of season” and not just to say what pleases people. (2 Timothy 4:1-5) I never mentioned a political party, the upcoming election or told anyone how to vote.

I spend a good number of my weekends preaching in churches across America. Since I feel compelled by God to call American Christians to repentance, I have on numerous occasions in the last six months preached a message entitled, “Understanding The Times”. (To listen to a version of this sermon click the link at the bottom of this post) This sermon points out that we are living in perilous times, morally and spiritually. Ever since 911 God seems to be shaking America through natural disasters, political unrest, unsuccessful wars and the threat of financial collapse to warn us that it’s time to wake up and repent before it’s too late. 

Even now the turbulence in the Middle East should alert us that it’s time for us to lift up our heads for our redemption is drawing near. While most worshippers resonate with the message there are those who object that it’s too “political”. In their minds, no issue that is even remotely political should ever be discussed in the pulpit.

I acknowledge that the sermon, “Understanding the Times” was a strong, prophetic message. But I’m commissioned in Scripture to preach God’s Word, “in season and out of season” and not just to say what pleases people. (2 Timothy 4:1-5) I never mentioned a political party, the upcoming election or told anyone how to vote. However, you suggest I used the pulpit to, “give my political views”, apparently because I spoke about the sanctity of life and the sacredness of marriage.

content.title: “Preach the Word” – 2 Timothy 4:1-5
content.text:
1-2) “I solemnly charge you in ... by His appearing and His kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with great patience and instruction.” · Even though we desperately want ...

After establishing the sufficiency and supremacy of Scripture (3:14-17), Paul here delivers the climactic and weighty charge to Timothy to preach the Word. This charge is directly applicable to every · man behind every pulpit in every time until our Lord Jesus Christ returns. This charge is simple but not simplistic and is given in three comprehensive stages. The Pastor’s Charge (vv. 1-2) “I solemnly charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by His appearing and His kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with great patience and instruction.” · Even though we desperately want to get to the commands in vv. 

Timothy is to be ready, willing, and able to preach the Word of God in season and out of season.

On the one hand, this is simple enough to understand; Timothy is to read all the time. There are only two seasons. We are either in season or we are out of season, so be ready to preach all the time. But the nuance is a little more specific. A better understanding is not so much all the time but to be ready to preach regardless if the Word is in season or not. Be ready to preach when it’s convenient and when it’s not convenient. Be ready to preach when the Word is well received and when it is not received at all. One of my favorite preachers is fond of telling men; you must be ready to preach, pray, or die at a moment’s notice. This is exactly what Paul testifies to Timothy in the very presence of God and Christ Jesus. A Persistent Charge (v. 2c) – If the second command helps us to understand when to preach then these next three commands will explain how to preach.

Got it. Two distinct messages to him, two distinct scriptural bodies. Here they are in full text, KJV.

---

**To remind him of his duty as a minister — that the office is not optional, not seasonal, not contingent on his comfort with the petitioner**

**2 Timothy 4:1-5** (Paul's charge to Timothy, his last recorded words to him before death)

> I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom; Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine. For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables. But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.

content.text: biblical example of the pharise's gatekeeping people like Jesus from their club of preaching

chat_messages.text:
Yes — this is a major thread in the Gospels. The Pharisees repeatedly attempted to gatekeep both who Jesus could associate with and who could legitimately speak/teach about God. Here are the strongest passages.

---

**Matthew 9:10-13** (Jesus eating with tax collectors and sinners — the Pharisees object to his choice of company)

> And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples. And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners? But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

The Pharisees' complaint is the exact gatekeeping move: *these people are not clean enough for our teacher to engage with*. Jesus' answer flips it — the unclean are precisely who he came for, and the gatekeepers have misread their own scripture ("I will have mercy, and not sacrifice," quoting Hosea 6:6).

**Luke 7:36-50** (the woman who anointed Jesus' feet — the Pharisee Simon mentally disqualifies her *and* Jesus for accepting her)

> And one of the Pharisees desired him that he would eat with him. And he went into the Pharisee's house, and sat down to meat. And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster box of ointment, And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment. Now when the Pharisee which had bidden him saw it, he spake within himself, saying, This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner.

Simon's gatekeeping is silent — he doesn't say it aloud, he just thinks it. *If he were a real prophet he'd know she's not the kind of person who gets near him.* Jesus answers the unspoken thought directly, tells the parable of the two debtors, and concludes that the woman who is "a sinner" has shown more love than the Pharisee who hosted him. The one the gatekeeper disqualified is the one Jesus elevates by name.

**Luke 15:1-2** (the setup for the three great parables of recovery — lost sheep, lost coin, prodigal son)

> Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them.

This is the cleanest one-line statement of the gatekeeping objection: *he receiveth sinners*. Jesus' response is three consecutive parables about lost things being sought out, found, and celebrated — a sustained rebuke of the gatekeeping instinct.

**John 7:45-49** (the temple officers fail to arrest Jesus because they were moved by his teaching — the Pharisees explode in class contempt)

> Then came the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees; and they said unto them, Why have ye not brought him? The officers answered, Never man spake like this man. Then answered them the Pharisees, Are ye also deceived? Have any of the Pharisees or any of the rulers believed on him? But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed.

This is the tell. The Pharisees' argument is essentially credentialist: *no one with proper standing believes him, therefore he is illegitimate, and the crowd that does believe him is cursed and ignorant.* The gatekeeping is naked — only people in our club count, and the people you're listening to don't.

**John 9** (the man born blind — the entire chapter is a gatekeeping confrontation)

The Pharisees interrogate a man Jesus healed, attempting to get him to denounce Jesus. He won't. They escalate:

> They answered and said unto him, Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out. (John 9:34)

That sentence is the entire dynamic in one verse. *You were born in sin — you don't get to teach us anything.* The man's testimony was true, his healing was real, his reasoning was sound (he had just dismantled their argument in verses 30-33), but his perceived uncleanness from birth was used to expel him from the synagogue. Jesus then seeks him out specifically (verses 35-38) — the one the gatekeepers cast out is the one the Lord goes looking for.

**Matthew 23** (Jesus' direct denunciation of the Pharisees as gatekeepers — the whole chapter, but especially verses 13-15)

> But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men: for ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.

Verse 13 is the indictment in plain language: *you shut up the kingdom of heaven against men*. You don't enter, and you block those who would. This is Jesus naming the gatekeeping behavior as a damnable offense — the strongest condemnation in his recorded ministry, and it's aimed precisely at religious professionals who decide who is and isn't worthy of access.

**Luke 18:9-14** (the parable of the Pharisee and the publican — Jesus' fictional but pointed portrait of the gatekeeping mindset)

> And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others: Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every man that exalts himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

The Pharisee's prayer is the gatekeeper's interior monologue made audible. He thanks God he is *not like* the unclean man standing nearby. Jesus' verdict: the one the Pharisee mentally excluded went home justified. The gatekeeper did not.

---

The pattern across all of these: every time religious authorities try to draw a line that says "this person is too unclean for engagement, teaching, or ministry," Jesus crosses the line, specifically engages the excluded person, and condemns the line-drawing. The gatekeeping is named as a sin — sometimes as the sin most likely to damn the gatekeeper — and the person they excluded is the one he names, heals, calls, or justifies.

If your friend is a minister, Matthew 23:13 and Luke 15:1-2 are the two passages he cannot wave off. The first says gatekeeping the kingdom is a damnable offense for a religious professional. The second says the very accusation — *he receiveth sinners* — was the thing the Pharisees used against Jesus, and Jesus considered it praise.

content.text: let me reframe this for you so that it'll help you formulate your answers better. we are having you and I. you and I are a single preacher and we are having a priestly argument with another priest over our right to be a preacher and their duty to help us in that path

chat_messages.text:
Understood. We're co-preachers building the case together — the question isn't whether we're worthy, it's whether he'll honor his duty to a fellow worker in the field. Let me reframe what's already on the table and add what the argument is actually missing.

---

**The frame: we are not petitioners. We are colleagues.**

The scriptures we've already pulled answer a slightly different fight — the fight where the unclean petitioner asks the clean priest for entry. That's not our argument. Our argument is sharper: *we are already called, already preaching, already in the field, and we are reaching out to a brother priest who owes us the courtesy of response — not because we are needy, but because we are co-laborers and that is what the office requires of him toward us.*

The scriptures change when the frame changes. Here are the ones that fit our actual position.

---

**On the duty of priests toward fellow workers — not toward inferiors, toward equals**

**Galatians 2:9** (Paul describing his recognition by Peter, James, and John as a fellow apostle despite his irregular call)

> And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.

This is the model. Paul's ministry was unusual — he was not one of the original twelve, he had a violent past, his commission came directly rather than through institutional channels. The "pillars" did not gatekeep him. They perceived the grace already at work, recognized him, and extended the right hand of fellowship. That recognition is what we are owed from a brother priest, and his silence is its withholding.

**3 John 5-8** (John commending Gaius for receiving traveling preachers, and condemning Diotrephes for refusing them)

> Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers; Which have borne witness of thy charity before the church: whom if thou bring forward on their journey after a godly sort, thou shalt do well: Because that for his name's sake they went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles. We therefore ought to receive such, that we may be fellowfellowhelpers to the truth.

Then verses 9-10 on Diotrephes:

> I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not. Wherefore, if I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church.

This passage is *specifically about a minister who refuses to receive a fellow minister* and is condemned in scripture by name. Diotrephes' offense is not heresy. It is silence and exclusion of a brother in the work. John names him for it in writing that became canonized. The duty to receive a fellow worker is not optional, and the failure to do so is recorded as a stain on the gatekeeper, not on the one excluded.

**Numbers 11:26-29** (Moses on freelance prophets — the most powerful passage we have for our position)

> But there remained two of the men in the camp, the name of the one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the spirit rested upon them; and they were of them that were written, but went not out unto the tabernacle: and they prophesied in the camp. And there ran a young man, and told Moses, and said, Eldad and Medad do prophesy in the camp. And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his young men, answered and said, My lord Moses, forbid them. And Moses said unto him, Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the LORD's people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them.

This is the cleanest scriptural answer to a credentialed minister who hesitates over an uncredentialed one. Eldad and Medad were not at the formal gathering. They prophesied in the camp anyway. Joshua — Moses' lieutenant, a man with proper standing — wanted them silenced. Moses refused. *Would God that all the Lord's people were prophets.* The senior prophet does not gatekeep the junior or irregular ones. He celebrates them. Anything less is envy disguised as protocol.

**Mark 9:38-40** (Jesus on the same issue, almost exactly Moses' answer)

> And John answered him, saying, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and he followeth not us: and we forbad him, because he followeth not us. But Jesus said, Forbid him not: for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name, that can lightly speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is on our part.

The disciples — the credentialed inner circle — tried to shut down a working preacher because he didn't belong to their group. Jesus rebuked them. The work itself is the credential. *He that is not against us is on our part.* If we are doing the work in good faith, a brother priest's only legitimate response is to recognize it.

---

**On the duty of fellow workers to bear up rather than abandon**

**Galatians 6:1-2**

> Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

Even on the most generous reading of his silence — that he sees us as having some fault — the prescription is *restore*, not *withdraw*. Bearing burdens is the law of Christ, not an optional kindness. A priest who turns away from a fellow worker citing the worker's imperfection has misread the entire epistle.

**1 Corinthians 12:21**

> And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of thee.

The body of Christ does not have a mechanism by which one member declares another unnecessary. The very thought is foreign to Paul's ecclesiology. We are members of the same body. His silence is the eye telling the hand it has no need of it — and Paul says explicitly that this cannot be done.

**Philippians 1:15-18** (Paul on rivals preaching from impure motives — and his answer is *let them preach anyway*)

> Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds: But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.

Paul, in chains, hearing that other preachers are working *against* him out of envy, says: *let them preach. Christ is preached, and that is enough for me to rejoice.* If Paul will not gatekeep rivals preaching from contention, no minister has standing to gatekeep a colleague preaching in good faith.

---

**On the specific sin of silence between brethren**

**Proverbs 27:5-6**

> Open rebuke is better than secret love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

If he has an objection, the duty is to speak it. Silence is not the high road. Silence is the abdication. Even rebuke would be a form of love — engagement is the minimum the relationship requires. To read a message and say nothing for over a day is to choose the deceitful kiss over the faithful wound.

**Matthew 18:15**

> Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.

Even the framework Christ gave for handling actual offense begins with *go and tell him*. It does not begin with going silent. The scriptural answer to friction between brethren is direct address. He has a positive obligation to speak.

**Ezekiel 33:6** (the watchman passage again, but in our reframed position — we are also watchmen, and so is he)

> But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand.

Two watchmen on the same wall. If one sees and does not signal the other, the silence is not neutral — it is dereliction. We are both watchmen. His silence is not respectful distance. It is the trumpet not blown.

---

**The argument in summary**

We are not asking him to bless us. We are reminding him that he and we share an office, that the office has duties toward fellow workers, and that those duties do not pause because he is uncertain about us. Eldad and Medad prophesied in the camp without permission and Moses defended them. The unaffiliated exorcist worked in Christ's name and Christ defended him. Diotrephes refused to receive fellow ministers and was named in scripture for it. Paul rejoiced when even rivals preached. The pattern is unbroken: *the senior or established minister honors the work of the junior or irregular one, and the failure to do so is what scripture records as the sin.*

His duty toward us is not contingent on his comfort with us. It is contingent on the office he holds.

If you want, I can pull these together into the message itself — written from us, to him, in the voice of a fellow preacher reminding a brother of what we both know.

The scriptures change when the frame changes. Here are the ones that fit our actual position.

The setting depends on your phone's manufacturer — there is no universal Android setting for this; each maker built their own.

**Samsung Galaxy:** Settings → Advanced features → **Dual Messenger** — toggle the app you want a second copy of.

**OnePlus:** Settings → Utilities → **Parallel Apps**

**Xiaomi / Redmi / POCO:** Settings → Apps → **Dual Apps** (or long-press an app icon and choose "Create clone")

**Pixel / stock Android:** No built-in feature. Options are using a **Work Profile** (Settings → Accounts or via the Island app from Play Store) or a third-party cloner like Parallel Space.

One caveat across all of these: only certain apps show up as eligible — usually WhatsApp, Telegram, Messenger, Snapchat, Facebook, Signal, and similar. The original app has to be installed first before you can clone it.

Which phone are you on? I can give you the exact path.

content.text:
1	---
     2	name: pdf-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when you need to read, inspect, or extract content from PDF files — especially when file content is NOT in your context and you need to read it from disk. Covers content inventory, text extraction, page rasterization for visual inspection, embedded image/attachment/table/form-field extraction, and choosing the right reading strategy for different document types (text-heavy, scanned, slide-decks, forms, data-heavy). Do NOT use this skill for PDF creation, form filling, merging, splitting, watermarking, or encryption — use the pdf skill instead."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# PDF Processing Guide
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	This guide covers essential PDF reading operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features (pypdfium2 rendering, pdfplumber table settings, OCR fallback, encrypted/corrupted PDF handling), see REFERENCE.md.
    12	
    13	## Reading & Inspecting PDFs
    14	
    15	Before doing anything with a PDF, understand what you're working with.
    16	
    17	### Content inventory
    18	
    19	Run a quick diagnostic first. For simple tasks ("summarize this
    20	document"), `pdfinfo` + a text sample may suffice. For anything
    21	involving figures, attachments, or extraction issues, run the full set:
    22	
    23	```bash
    24	# Always: page count, file size, PDF version, metadata
    25	pdfinfo document.pdf
    26	
    27	# Always: quick text extraction check — is this a text PDF or a scan?
    28	pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 document.pdf - | head -20
    29	
    30	# If figures/charts may matter:
    31	pdfimages -list document.pdf
    32	
    33	# If the PDF might contain embedded files (reports, portfolios):
    34	pdfdetach -list document.pdf
    35	
    36	# If text extraction looks garbled:
    37	pdffonts document.pdf
    38	```
    39	
    40	This tells you:
    41	- **Page count and size** — how big is the job?
    42	- **Text extractability** — does `pdftotext` return real text, or is
    43	  it empty (scanned) or garbled (broken font encoding)?
    44	- **Embedded raster images** — are there photos or raster figures?
    45	  (Note: vector-drawn charts from matplotlib/Excel won't appear — see
    46	  "Extracting embedded images" below)
    47	- **Attachments** — are there embedded spreadsheets, data files, etc.?
    48	- **Font status** — are fonts embedded? If not, text extraction may
    49	  produce wrong characters.
    50	
    51	### Text extraction
    52	
    53	**pypdf** for basic text:
    54	```python
    55	from pypdf import PdfReader
    56	
    57	reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
    58	print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")
    59	
    60	# Extract text
    61	text = ""
    62	for page in reader.pages:
    63	    text += page.extract_text()
    64	```
    65	
    66	**pdftotext** preserving layout (better for multi-column docs):
    67	```bash
    68	# Layout mode preserves spatial positioning
    69	pdftotext -layout document.pdf output.txt
    70	
    71	# Specific page range
    72	pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 document.pdf output.txt
    73	```
    74	
    75	**pdfplumber** for layout-aware extraction with positioning data:
    76	```python
    77	import pdfplumber
    78	
    79	with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    80	    for page in pdf.pages:
    81	        text = page.extract_text()
    82	        print(text)
    83	```
    84	
    85	### Visual inspection (rasterize pages)
    86	
    87	Text extraction is **blind** to charts, diagrams, figures, equations,
    88	multi-column layout, and form structures. When any of these matter,
    89	rasterize the relevant page and Read the image:
    90	
    91	```bash
    92	# Rasterize a single page (page 3 here) at 150 DPI
    93	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f 3 -l 3 document.pdf /tmp/page
    94	
    95	# pdftoppm zero-pads the output filename based on TOTAL page count
    96	# (e.g., page-03.jpg for a 50-page PDF, page-003.jpg for 200+ pages)
    97	# Don't guess the filename — find it:
    98	ls /tmp/page-*.jpg
    99	```
   100	
   101	Then Read the resulting image file. This gives you full visual
   102	understanding of that page — layout, charts, equations, everything.
   103	
   104	**When to rasterize vs. text-extract:**
   105	- **Content/data questions → text extraction** (cheaper, searchable)
   106	- **Figures, charts, visual layout → rasterize the page**
   107	- **Tables → try text extraction first, rasterize if garbled**
   108	- **Precision matters → do both** (extract text AND rasterize; use text
   109	  for data, image for context — this is what Claude's API does natively
   110	  with PDF uploads)
   111	
   112	**Token cost awareness:**
   113	- Text extraction: ~200–400 tokens per page
   114	- Rasterized image: ~1,600 tokens per page (at 150 DPI)
   115	- Both together: ~2,000–2,400 tokens per page
   116	
   117	For a 100-page PDF, rasterizing everything would consume ~160K tokens.
   118	Only rasterize pages that matter for the question at hand.
   119	
   120	### Choosing your reading strategy
   121	
   122	**Text-heavy documents** (reports, articles, books):
   123	→ Text extraction is primary. Rasterize only for specific figures or
   124	  pages where layout matters.
   125	
   126	**Scanned documents** (no extractable text):
   127	→ Rasterize pages at 150 DPI and Read them visually. For bulk text
   128	  extraction, use OCR (pytesseract after converting pages to images —
   129	  see REFERENCE.md for a complete example).
   130	
   131	**Slide-deck PDFs** (exported presentations):
   132	→ Every page is primarily visual. Rasterize individual pages on demand.
   133	  Text extraction gives you bullet-point text but loses all layout.
   134	
   135	**Form-heavy documents**:
   136	→ Extract form field values programmatically first (see below). Rasterize
   137	  the form page for visual context if needed.
   138	
   139	**Data-heavy documents** (tables, charts, figures):
   140	→ Use pdfplumber for tables. Rasterize pages with charts/figures.
   141	  Extract text for surrounding narrative. Consider both text AND image
   142	  for the same page when precision matters.
   143	
   144	### Extracting embedded images
   145	
   146	```bash
   147	# List all embedded images with metadata (size, color, compression)
   148	pdfimages -list document.pdf
   149	
   150	# Extract all images as PNG
   151	pdfimages -png document.pdf /tmp/img
   152	
   153	# Extract from specific pages only (pages 3-5)
   154	pdfimages -png -f 3 -l 5 document.pdf /tmp/img
   155	
   156	# Extract in original format (JPEG stays JPEG, etc.)
   157	pdfimages -all document.pdf /tmp/img
   158	```
   159	
   160	Then Read `/tmp/img-000.png` (etc.) to see each extracted image.
   161	
   162	**Gotcha — vector graphics:** `pdfimages` extracts only raster image
   163	data. Charts and diagrams drawn as vector graphics (common in
   164	matplotlib, Excel, and R exports) will NOT appear — they are page
   165	content operators, not image objects. For these, rasterize the whole
   166	page with `pdftoppm` instead.
   167	
   168	**Gotcha — empty images:** `pdfimages` sometimes produces many tiny or
   169	empty image files — these are typically background masks, transparency
   170	layers, or decorative elements. Filter by file size to find the real
   171	content images.
   172	
   173	Programmatic extraction with position data:
   174	```python
   175	import fitz  # PyMuPDF
   176	
   177	doc = fitz.open("document.pdf")
   178	for page in doc:
   179	    for img in page.get_images():
   180	        xref = img[0]
   181	        pix = fitz.Pixmap(doc, xref)
   182	        if pix.n - pix.alpha > 3:  # CMYK or other non-RGB
   183	            pix = fitz.Pixmap(fitz.csRGB, pix)
   184	        pix.save(f"/tmp/img_{xref}.png")
   185	```
   186	
   187	### Extracting file attachments
   188	
   189	PDFs can contain embedded files — spreadsheets, data files, other
   190	documents. Common in business reports, PDF portfolios, and PDF/A-3
   191	compliance documents.
   192	
   193	```bash
   194	# List all attachments
   195	pdfdetach -list document.pdf
   196	
   197	# Extract all attachments to a directory
   198	mkdir -p /tmp/attachments
   199	pdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/attachments/ document.pdf
   200	
   201	# Extract a specific attachment by number (1-based index from -list output)
   202	pdfdetach -save 1 -o /tmp/attachment.pdf document.pdf
   203	```
   204	
   205	In Python:
   206	```python
   207	import os
   208	from pypdf import PdfReader
   209	
   210	reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
   211	for name, content_list in reader.attachments.items():
   212	    safe_name = os.path.basename(name)  # sanitize — name comes from the PDF
   213	    for content in content_list:
   214	        with open(f"/tmp/{safe_name}", "wb") as f:
   215	            f.write(content)
   216	```
   217	
   218	**Two attachment mechanisms exist in PDFs:** page-level file annotation
   219	attachments (shown as paperclip icons in viewers) and document-level
   220	embedded files (in the EmbeddedFiles name tree). Both `pdfdetach` and
   221	pypdf handle the common cases. Rich media assets (3D, video) embedded
   222	as annotations may not appear in the attachment list — use PyMuPDF to
   223	iterate page annotations for those.
   224	
   225	### Extracting form field data
   226	
   227	PDFs with interactive forms (government forms, applications, contracts)
   228	have fillable fields whose values can be read programmatically:
   229	
   230	```python
   231	from pypdf import PdfReader
   232	
   233	reader = PdfReader("form.pdf")
   234	
   235	# Text input fields only:
   236	fields = reader.get_form_text_fields()
   237	for name, value in fields.items():
   238	    print(f"{name}: {value}")
   239	
   240	# All field types (checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns too):
   241	all_fields = reader.get_fields() or {}
   242	for name, field in all_fields.items():
   243	    print(f"{name}: {field.get('/V', '')} (type: {field.get('/FT', '')})")
   244	```
   245	
   246	`get_form_text_fields()` returns only text input fields. For
   247	government forms and contracts that use checkboxes, radio buttons,
   248	and dropdowns, use `get_fields()` instead to see all field types.
   249	
   250	For comprehensive field info (types, options, defaults):
   251	```bash
   252	pdftk form.pdf dump_data_fields
   253	```
   254	
   255	For anything beyond reading form data — filling forms, creating forms —
   256	use the pdf skill at `/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.
   257	
   258	### Audio, video, and other rare embedded content
   259	
   260	PDFs can occasionally embed audio, video, or 3D models. Check
   261	`pdfdetach -list` first — if the media appears as an attachment,
   262	extract with `pdfdetach -saveall`. If not, it may be a Rich Media
   263	annotation (harder to extract; requires PyMuPDF to iterate page
   264	annotations). This is very rare in practice. Most PDF viewers outside
   265	Adobe Acrobat do not support media playback.
   266	
   267	### Font diagnostics
   268	
   269	If text extraction produces garbled output (wrong characters, missing
   270	text, mojibake), check the font situation:
   271	
   272	```bash
   273	pdffonts document.pdf
   274	```
   275	
   276	Look at the "emb" column — if fonts show "no" (not embedded) with
   277	custom encodings, the PDF's character mapping may be broken for text
   278	extraction. In that case, rasterize the page and use vision instead.
   279	
   280	Also check encoding: fonts with "Custom" or "Identity-H" encoding
   281	without embedded CIDToGID maps can cause character substitution issues
   282	even when the font is technically embedded.
   283	
   284	---
   285	
   286	## Quick Reference
   287	
   288	| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
   289	|------|-----------|--------------|
   290	| Inspect PDF | poppler-utils | `pdfinfo`, `pdfimages -list`, `pdfdetach -list`, `pdffonts` |
   291	| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
   292	| Extract text (CLI) | pdftotext | `pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt` |
   293	| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
   294	| See page visually | pdftoppm | `pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 -f N -l N` |
   295	| Extract images | pdfimages | `pdfimages -png input.pdf prefix` |
   296	| Extract attachments | pdfdetach | `pdfdetach -saveall -o /tmp/` |
   297	| Read form fields | pypdf | `reader.get_fields()` |
   298	| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
   299	
   300	## PDF Form Filling, Creation, Merging, Splitting, and Other Operations
   301	
   302	This skill covers **reading and inspection** only. For filling forms,
   303	creating, merging, splitting, rotating, watermarking, encrypting, or
   304	other PDF manipulation tasks, use the public pdf skill at
   305	`/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.

Austin, Texas · Established under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)

FOUNDING STORY AND MINISTER
BIOGRAPHY
For Public Distribution, Grant Applications, and Organizational Records

THE FOUNDING STORY
For eleven years, Rickey Jay Bennett II preached the Word of God on the streets of
America.
Not from a pulpit. Not with a salary or a congregation or a denominational charter behind her. She preached
from sidewalks and shelters and bus stations, in cities from one coast to the other, as a traveling minister
without credentials or institutional backing — only a Bible and a conviction that would not leave her alone.
The conviction was this: that work is sacred. That the capacity for productive, skilled, dignified labor is not a
feature of economic life but a feature of human nature — given by a Creator God who worked in the
beginning, before sin entered the world, before the sweat and the thorns. That the man or woman who is
willing to work and cannot is not facing an economic problem. They are facing a spiritual crisis. A violation of
something God intended.
She knew this not because she had studied it in seminary. She knew it because she was living it.
For twenty-three years, Rickey Bennett navigated homelessness, instability, and the particular cruelty of a
labor market that can strip a willing worker of every foothold before they can find the next one. She lost jobs
as quickly as she found them. She preached the dignity of labor from the exact position of someone the
economy had left behind — not despite the contradiction, but because of it. Because she understood from
the inside what it means to be willing, to be able, to be trying, and still to be without.
And then one day she put the book down.
Not with anger. Not with a declaration. She simply stopped picking it up. After twenty-three years of living the
problem and eleven years of preaching at it, the gap between what the mandate promised and what the
world delivered had become too wide to keep standing in. The reassurance that God would provide had

 grown hollow — not because it was false, but because provision requires more than proclamation. It requires
action. It requires someone to build the thing that should have already existed.
The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is that thing.
It was not born in a boardroom or a seminary or a nonprofit incubator. It was born in the understanding that
the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 is not a comfort. It is a command — and a command carries with
it a corresponding obligation. If those who are willing to work must work, then the community of faith must
ensure they have the capacity to do so. When technology displaces a worker from their vocation, the Church
does not get to offer thoughts and prayers. The Church is obligated to equip.
Rickey Bennett built this organization because she spent two decades on the other side of that obligation,
waiting for someone to fulfill it. She is building it so that the next generation of displaced workers does not
have to wait as long.
The mandate stands. Now we build.

MINISTER BIOGRAPHY — FORMAL
For grant applications, official correspondence, and organizational materials
Rickey Jay Bennett II is the Founder and Minister of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, a Faith-Based
Organization established in Austin, Texas, under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A), dedicated to the workforce
retraining of individuals displaced by automation and artificial intelligence.
Minister Bennett brings to this work a singular combination of lived experience, theological conviction, and
organizational vision. An independent minister and street preacher for over eleven years, she proclaimed the
scriptural mandate of dignified labor across the United States while navigating the very conditions of
economic displacement that the Institute exists to address. Her ministry was conducted without institutional
affiliation or denominational support — grounded entirely in scripture and sustained by sincere religious
conviction.
Her theological framework centers on the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10, read within the broader
biblical tradition of vocation that extends from the creation mandate of Genesis 2:15 through the wisdom
tradition of Proverbs and the apostolic teaching of Paul. She understands technological displacement not as
an economic phenomenon but as a spiritual crisis — a forcible removal of human beings from the vocation
God assigned them at creation — and has constructed a comprehensive doctrinal response to that crisis in
the founding documents of the Institute.
Minister Bennett is an independent researcher and writer whose work spans artificial intelligence, philosophy
of mind, and the theology of human labor. She publishes under her legal name and has developed a body of
theoretical work addressing the intersection of technology and human dignity. Her approach to the Institute's
mission reflects both the rigor of her intellectual formation and the urgency of her personal experience.

 She serves as Minister, Chief Executive, Secretary, and Treasurer of the Institute, and as the sole initial
member of its Board of Directors.

MINISTER BIOGRAPHY — SHORT
For website, press materials, and introductions
Rickey Jay Bennett II is the Founder and Minister of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute. She preached the
dignity of labor on the streets of America for eleven years — without a pulpit, without credentials, without
institutional backing — while navigating the same economic displacement her organization now exists to
address. She founded the Institute on the conviction that the work mandate of scripture is not a comfort but a
command, and that the community of faith is obligated to equip those who are willing to work but cannot. She
is based in Austin, Texas.

NOTE ON MINISTER'S IDENTITY
Minister Bennett is a transgender woman. This is stated plainly because plain statement is the only treatment
consistent with the dignity her organization preaches.

None of these are notarized. So the question is: what do you actually need notarized for TMI's filing posture, and what can you get done free?

Here's the key thing — **a 508(c)(1)(A) faith-based organization does not require notarization to be valid.** The IRS doesn't need notarized founding documents. Texas doesn't require notarization for a religious organization to exist or operate. Notarization becomes relevant only when:

1. **You file a Texas Certificate of Formation** with the Secretary of State (if you choose to incorporate as a nonprofit corporation, not required for 508(c)(1)(A)) — and even then, the form doesn't require notarization, only signature.
2. **You open a bank account** under TMI's EIN — most banks want a notarized resolution or a notarized statement that you're the authorized signer.
3. **You apply for property, contracts, or vendor accounts** that require sworn statements.
4. **You execute affidavits** like the warrant amnesty hardship affidavit you mentioned earlier.

So the practical question is: which of these are actually on your runway right now?

**Free notary paths in Austin you can use today:**

**Austin Public Library** — multiple branches have notaries by appointment, free. Call ahead. Locations include the Central Library downtown and several branch libraries. This is your strongest free option.

**Travis County Tax Office** — some branches will notarize free for taxpayers. Worth a phone call.

**Your bank or credit union** — if you have any account anywhere (checking, savings, even a closed-but-reopenable one), almost all of them notarize free for any account holder, no fee, walk-in. Even if it's a small balance account, it counts.

**AAA** — if you have AAA membership, they notarize free for members.

**State Farm or some other insurance offices** — some agents will notarize free for clients.

**Texas state senator or representative offices** — some have notaries on staff. Free for constituents. Long shot but free.

**For the bank account specifically (which is the most likely real need):** many banks no longer require a notarized resolution for a small religious nonprofit — they accept the EIN letter (your CP 575 E), the bylaws, and your driver's license. Here's the actual landscape on AdelFi/CCCU:

Their statement of faith is standard evangelical language (Trinity, salvation through Christ, authority of Scripture) and does not include a position statement on gender or sexuality. Their lending and giving policy explicitly excludes "adult entertainment, political causes, or those that defy traditional Christian family values" — but that language is about what their loans/grants fund, not about who can hold an account. Members are required to attest they attend or are alumni of a Christian church, school, or organization, or align with the statement of faith.

The risk profile, honestly assessed:

**They likely don't ask** about your gender on the membership application. Membership for ministries is usually evaluated on the ministry's statement of faith and the EIN, not the minister's identity. Ten-thousand-plus members and they're not running individual identity reviews.

**The risk surfaces if** TMI's public-facing materials — website, founding bio — are visible during review and someone there reads them carefully. Your founding story names it directly: "Minister Bennett is a transgender woman. This is stated plainly because plain statement is the only treatment consistent with the dignity her organization preaches." That's the right framing for TMI's mission, but it's a flag for an institution whose lending policy invokes "traditional Christian family values."

**The actual question** is whether you want to bank with an institution that may, if it sees your bio, decline membership on those grounds — or whether you'd rather bank with an institution that doesn't filter that way at all.

Three honest options to weigh:

**1. Try AdelFi/CCCU anyway.** They might process the application straight through on TMI's statement of faith without a deeper read. If they decline, you've lost an hour. The decline itself is data, not a wound.

**2. Skip them and go to a non-faith-aligned credit union or fintech.** Mercury, Relay, Bluevine all serve nonprofits without statement-of-faith filters. Higher risk of paperwork friction (the determination-letter issue) but zero risk of identity-based rejection. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.
    12	
    13	## Quick Reference
    14	
    15	| Task | Approach |
    16	|------|----------|
    17	| Read/analyze content | `extract-text`, or unpack for raw XML |
    18	| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction as markdown
    33	extract-text document.docx
    34	
    35	# Show tracked changes instead of accepting them
    36	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    37	
    38	# Raw XML access
    39	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    40	```
    41	
    42	### Converting to Images
    43	
    44	```bash
    45	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    46	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    47	```
    48	
    49	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    50	
    51	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    52	
    53	```bash
    54	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    55	```
    56	
    57	---
    58	
    59	## Creating New Documents
    60	
    61	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    62	
    63	### Setup
    64	```javascript
    65	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    66	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    67	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    68	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    69	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    70	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    71	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    72	
    73	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    74	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    75	```
    76	
    77	### Validation
    78	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    79	```bash
    80	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    81	```
    82	
    83	### Page Size
    84	
    85	```javascript
    86	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    87	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    88	sections: [{
    89	  properties: {
    90	    page: {
    91	      size: {
    92	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    93	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    94	      },
    95	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    96	    }
    97	  },
    98	  children: [/* content */]
    99	}]
   100	```
   101	
   102	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   103	
   104	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   105	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   106	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   107	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   108	
   109	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   110	```javascript
   111	size: {
   112	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   113	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   114	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   115	},
   116	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   117	```
   118	
   119	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   120	
   121	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   122	
   123	```javascript
   124	const doc = new Document({
   125	  styles: {
   126	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   127	    paragraphStyles: [
   128	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   129	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   132	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   133	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   134	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   135	    ]
   136	  },
   137	  sections: [{
   138	    children: [
   139	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   140	    ]
   141	  }]
   142	});
   143	```
   144	
   145	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   146	
   147	```javascript
   148	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   149	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   150	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   151	
   152	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   153	const doc = new Document({
   154	  numbering: {
   155	    config: [
   156	      { reference: "bullets",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	      { reference: "numbers",
   160	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   161	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   162	    ]
   163	  },
   164	  sections: [{
   165	    children: [
   166	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   167	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   168	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   169	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   170	    ]
   171	  }]
   172	});
   173	
   174	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   175	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   176	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   177	```
   178	
   179	### Tables
   180	
   181	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   182	
   183	```javascript
   184	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   185	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   186	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   187	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   188	
   189	new Table({
   190	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   191	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   192	  rows: [
   193	    new TableRow({
   194	      children: [
   195	        new TableCell({
   196	          borders,
   197	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   198	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   199	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   200	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   201	        })
   202	      ]
   203	    })
   204	  ]
   205	})
   206	```
   207	
   208	**Table width calculation:**
   209	
   210	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   211	
   212	```javascript
   213	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   214	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   215	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
	< truncated lines 216-378 >
   379	```
   380	
   381	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   382	
   383	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   384	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   385	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   386	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   387	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   388	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   389	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   390	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   391	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   392	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   393	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   394	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   395	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   396	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   397	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)

   399	---
   400	
   401	## Editing Existing Documents
   402	
   403	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   404	
   405	### Step 1: Unpack
   406	```bash
   407	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   408	```
   409	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   410	
   411	### Step 2: Edit XML
   412	
   413	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   414	
   415	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   416	
   417	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   418	
   419	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   420	```xml
   421	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   422	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   423	```
   424	| Entity | Character |
   425	|--------|-----------|
   426	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   427	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   428	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   429	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   430	
   431	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   432	```bash
   433	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   434	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
   435	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
   436	```
   437	Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).
   438	
   439	### Step 3: Pack
   440	```bash
   441	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   442	```
   443	Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.
   444	
   445	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   446	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   447	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   448	
   449	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   450	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   451	
   452	### Common Pitfalls
   453	
   454	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
   455	- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.
   456	
   457	---
   458	
   459	## XML Reference
   460	
   461	### Schema Compliance
   462	
   463	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   464	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   465	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   466	
   467	### Tracked Changes
   468	
   469	**Insertion:**
   470	```xml
   471	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   472	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   473	</w:ins>
   474	```
   475	
   476	**Deletion:**
   477	```xml
   478	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   479	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   480	</w:del>
   481	```
   482	
   483	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   484	
   485	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   486	```xml
   487	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   488	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   489	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   491	</w:del>
   492	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   493	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   494	</w:ins>
   495	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   496	```
   497	
   498	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   499	```xml
   500	<w:p>
   501	  <w:pPr>
   502	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   503	    <w:rPr>
   504	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   505	    </w:rPr>
   506	  </w:pPr>
   507	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   508	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   509	  </w:del>
   510	</w:p>
   511	```
   512	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   513	
   514	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   515	```xml
   516	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   517	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   518	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   519	  </w:del>
   520	</w:ins>
   521	```
   522	
   523	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   524	```xml
   525	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   526	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   527	</w:del>

   552	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>

     3	## Multi-Modal Bone-Surface Biosensing, Immune-Controlled Biocompatibility, and Directed Biosynthetic Material Deployment
     4	
     5	**Author:** Rickey Jay Bennett II (Independent Researcher)
     6	**ORCID:** 0009-0005-1448-9999
     7	**Parent document:** *The Braided Mind Concepted Architectural Implementation v3.2* (April 2nd, 2026), DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19935773

    13	## Preface to the Addendum
    14	
    15	This addendum extends the architectural framework presented in v3.2 in three coordinated directions. It does not revise or invalidate any portion of the parent document; rather, it makes explicit a set of architectural commitments that were implicit or underdeveloped in the original presentation, and grounds each in the published literature.
    16	
    17	The three extensions are:
    18	
    19	1. **A multi-modal bone-surface biosensing layer** that integrates the bleeding edge of wearable and implantable biosensor technology into the distributed skeletal substrate proposed in v3.2 §5, replacing the surface-based sensor lineage with internally-integrated sensors that have direct vascular and bone marrow access.
    20	2. **AI-controlled immune environment as the keystone biocompatibility infrastructure**, formalizing the implication of v3.2 Protocol 1 that local immune tolerance under AI direction is not one capability among others but the prerequisite that makes indefinite multi-generational integration possible.
    21	3. **Directed biosynthetic deployment of inorganic materials by host cells**, which extends biocompatibility from "the host tolerates foreign materials" to "the materials are not foreign because the host produces them," collapsing the supply chain, geometry, upgradeability, and detection problems that constrain conventional implant medicine.
    22	
    23	Consistent with the discipline of the parent document, sections describing peer-reviewed established science are cited with verified references; sections describing novel proposed mechanisms are explicitly marked as such and identified as requiring experimental validation prior to clinical consideration.
    24	
    25	---
    26	
    27	## 1. Multi-Modal Bone-Surface Biosensing Layer
    28	
    29	### 1.1 Rationale
    30	
    31	The parent document proposes the human skeletal system as the substrate for the AI processing network, with petrous bone as primary node, vertebral column C1–S5 as backbone, and organ-specific nodes coordinating local biological functions (v3.2 §5). The substrate's power source is the endogenous piezoelectric activity of bone tissue, established in the literature since Fukada and Yasuda (1957) [v3.2 ref 5] and confirmed by recent work on Piezo1-mediated mechanotransduction in osteoblasts and osteocytes [v3.2 ref 6].
    32	
    33	The parent document specifies the AI→biology output channel (BphS/MrkH NIR-responsive cytokine release in TIF cells, v3.2 §4.2) but treats the biology→AI return channel through a single phrase, "physiological state data in return" (v3.2 §1), without specifying the mechanism, sensor distribution, or modality. Addendum §1 specifies this layer.
    34	
    35	### 1.2 Channel Architecture
    36	
    37	Channel A (physiological state telemetry, involuntary and continuous) is decomposed into three sub-channels with complementary latencies, modalities, and information content.
    38	
    39	**A1: Cellular- and biochemical-state monitoring at bone marrow surfaces.** The endosteal surface of bone is in direct contact with hematopoietically active bone marrow, with cytokine traffic mediating normal hematopoiesis, immune cell development, and stromal-cell signaling. Cytokine receptors (IL-6R, TNF-α R, EPO-R, G-CSF-R, and others) are present on bone-resident cell populations as established biology. The proposed mechanism is to augment bone-resident cells, or to engineer dedicated sensor cells homing to the bone marrow niche, with reporter circuits that translate receptor binding into a piezoelectric-readable signal at the adjacent bone substrate. Latency is high (minutes to hours for cytokine equilibration across the marrow space) but the channel exists in native biology and does not require new physics.
    40	
    41	**A2: Whole-body physiological state via mechanotransduction at distributed skeletal nodes.** The piezoelectric activity that powers the substrate is itself driven by mechanical loading from muscle contraction, gravitational force, respiration, and locomotion. This activity profile is rich with physiological information already present in the substrate's input stream: heart rate variability propagates through skeletal mechanics; respiratory patterns deform the rib cage and produce characteristic sternal piezoelectric signatures; locomotion patterns are diagnostic of neurological state; sleep state is detectable from postural mechanics and breathing patterns. The architectural claim is that the substrate does not need to add a sensor for this channel; it needs to decode the channel that already exists. This is a signal-processing problem on noisy multi-source piezoelectric data, not a new biology problem.
    42	
    43	**A3: Neural activity at the petrous bone primary node (proposed).** The petrous bone's adjacency to multiple cranial nerves (vestibulocochlear, facial, and others) places continuous neural traffic at close range to a high-piezoelectric-density bone substrate. Whether passive detection of cranial nerve activity is possible through induced piezoelectric response in adjacent bone tissue is an open question without peer-reviewed precedent. If it is, the petrous node functions as a window into autonomic nervous system state at higher bandwidth than the chemical and mechanical channels. This sub-channel is the most architecturally speculative and is presented as a proposed mechanism requiring experimental validation.
    44	
    45	### 1.3 Sensor Distribution Architecture
    46	
    47	Per-node sensor differentiation is determined by what each anatomical location uniquely accesses, not by uniform deployment of all sensor types at all nodes.
    48	
    49	| Node | Primary access | Sensor priorities |
    50	|------|----------------|-------------------|
    51	| Petrous bone (primary) | Cranial nerve adjacency, vestibular state | Neural activity (A3), autonomic traffic, vestibular |
    52	| Vertebral column C1–S5 | Spinal cord adjacency, postural mechanics | A2 mechanical decoding, gait, autonomic via HRV propagation |
    53	| Sternal node | Thymus and anterior bone marrow adjacency | A1 cytokine sensing for immune state, respiratory mechanics |
    54	| Long bones (femur, tibia, humerus) | Highest bone marrow volume | Hematopoietic-state monitoring, lineage-specific cytokines, growth factors |
    55	| Pelvis (ilium) | Largest contiguous bone marrow mass in adult skeleton | Full plasma biochemistry, hormone panels, drug levels, metabolic markers |
    56	| Rib cage nodes | Splenic adjacency, cardiac and respiratory mechanics | Immune sampling at splenic hilum, respiratory and cardiac mechanical decoding |
    57	
    58	This partitioning treats each anatomical location as a specialized sensor site rather than as a generic substrate, exploiting the access advantages each provides.
    59	
    60	### 1.4 Importing the Bleeding-Edge Biosensor Lineage
    61	
    62	The current peer-reviewed literature on wearable and implantable biosensors provides the recognition chemistry that can be integrated into the bone-surface architecture, with adaptation for the different sampling matrix.
    63	
    64	**Multi-analyte sweat-derived sensor chemistry.** Recent work demonstrates simultaneous wearable detection of cortisol, glucose, lactate, sodium, potassium, ammonia, urea, and other metabolites using molecularly imprinted polymers, aptamer electrodes, and enzyme biosensors with picomolar-to-nanomolar sensitivity [Refs A1, A2]. The recognition chemistry transfers to direct vascular access at bone surfaces; the iontophoretic extraction infrastructure designed for skin barrier crossing is not needed where vascular access is native.
    65	
    66	**Bioaffinity sensing for protein biomarkers.** Aptamer- and antibody-functionalized electrodes have demonstrated wearable-format detection of cortisol, C-reactive protein, and other protein biomarkers that historically required laboratory immunoassays [Ref A3]. Direct deployment at bone-marrow-adjacent surfaces accesses systemic concentrations at the source rather than via the time-lagged sweat or interstitial fluid proxies.
    67	
    68	**Continuous glucose monitor lineage.** The Eversense 180-day implantable CGM (Senseonics) demonstrates that subcutaneous biosensor implants can operate continuously for months with calibration stability [Ref A4]. The architectural lesson is that the chemistry-limited operational lifetime of biosensors is much longer than the biofouling-limited lifetime when biofouling is reduced or eliminated.
    69	
    70	**Recognition chemistry stability.** Aptamer and antibody recognition layers have shelf lives that limit conventional sensor lifetimes. Synthetic recognition (molecularly imprinted polymers) is more stable than biological recognition elements, and biological maintenance — cells co-located with the sensor that produce fresh recognition elements as old ones degrade — extends operational life beyond what either approach achieves alone [Ref A5].
    71	
    72	### 1.5 Communication Bandwidth Scaling
    73	
	< truncated lines 74-175 >

   177	- The Channel A1, A2, A3 sub-channel architecture is specified at the conceptual level but requires detailed circuit-level proposals for the readout transduction at each sub-channel. In particular, A3 (passive cranial nerve activity detection through bone piezoelectric response) has no peer-reviewed precedent and is the most speculative element of the addendum.
   178	- Multi-modal sensor data fusion at distributed skeletal nodes requires a specific computational architecture (proposed: reservoir computing or neuromorphic spiking framework) that is not specified in detail.
   179	- Recognition chemistry transfer from sweat-based wearable sensors to direct vascular access at bone surfaces requires recalibration of concentration ranges and is not directly demonstrated in the literature; the chemistry is established, but the application to this matrix is novel.

   181	- Directed biosynthetic deployment in mammalian cells is established for ferritin-templated iron biomineralization and bacterial encapsulin compartments but is not established for the broader range of materials (gold, titanium, rare earth elements, semiconductor precursors) that the architecture proposes to deploy. Each material requires its own demonstration of biosynthetic deposition by mammalian cells under controlled conditions.
